_Why can an agent lose the thread of a task even when its entire history still fits?_

An agent's context window is a finite and expensive resource, not an unbounded repository for raw text. Naively accumulating tool outputs, conversational turns, and retrieved snippets exhausts token capacity, inflates prefill latency, and spreads attention across material the next decision does not need. Fitting is not the same as being usable. A request that fits can still place a refuted hypothesis beside the test that refuted it, or present a result from an earlier revision as a fact about the current one. Effective context engineering treats each request as a deliberately selected working set, in which relevant state is compacted without losing its provenance, superseded observations are withdrawn, and bulky artifacts stay in durable storage behind handles. Stale or truncated evidence that does reach the model produces errors that compound across later turns. The systems challenge is to carry an accurate, minimal projection of the environment within the token budget, so that the state an agent carries bounds its uncertainty rather than compounding it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Distinguish nominal request capacity from usable working context and explain why admitted tokens dilute needed evidence
- Allocate the next request's input budget while preserving output headroom and task-relevant evidence
- Design a context layout that orders entries by change rate for prefix reuse and binds each observation to its evidential scope
- Compare compaction policies by information loss, recovery requirements, and the cost of repeated transformations
- Audit a progress record against runtime-owned sources and quantify how unchecked per-round constraint loss compounds across compaction cycles
- Apply dependency-aware invalidation without treating historical observations as proof of current state
- Evaluate context policies by decision quality, accepted outcomes, and total resource use under common limits

:::

## Carrying a Repair Across Turns {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-overview}

The repair agent (@sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses) has spent several turns investigating a connection-pool defect. It has inspected the pool implementation, executed a reproduction test, and revised its initial diagnosis. Deliberation has left behind candidate versions, a refuted timeout hypothesis, test observations, and the dependency records that tie them together (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision). None of that progress lives inside the model. Because foundation models are stateless functions across turns, every call begins and ends with the payload assembled by the host runtime. The agent can use the test trace, honor public API constraints, and avoid revisiting a rejected hypothesis only if the runtime includes them in the upcoming request. The runtime must also structure that request so that the status and role of each artifact remain unambiguous.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with only the State axis lit in purple."}

*Working context governs the within-session state exposure by selecting, representing, and refreshing what each call carries.*
:::

The token accounting of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization settles two questions for an individual request: whether the payload satisfies the admission bound, and what its tokens cost (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost). Those bounds, however, do not determine whether the prompt helps the model make a sound decision. A prompt can fit well within token limits and still fail to guide the agent toward a valid repair. The simplest agent architectures evade this problem by treating context as an append-only log, concatenating every observation, tool execution, and partial response into an expanding transcript. That policy breaks down almost immediately. Even while the transcript fits within physical limits, the runtime pays repeatedly for obsolete tokens that the next decision no longer requires. Stale code snippets sit alongside their replacements, and refuted hypotheses linger alongside the test results that disproved them, diluting the model's attention. When an extended trajectory inevitably exhausts the context window, an unmanaged runtime must truncate blindly, evicting instructions or early constraints without any principled criterion for what to preserve.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The quadratic input cost of resending an append-only history on every call is established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-trajectory-cost-accumulation.
:::

The agent's *working context* is the runtime subsystem that decides what each model call receives. Rather than treating context as a passive transcript, this subsystem constructs a bounded working set tailored to a single decision. It establishes token budgets for each distinct role in the prompt and arranges data layouts so unchanged prefixes can be reused across turns. It compacts historical evidence without distorting the facts, maintains structured progress records that resist summarization drift, and enforces invalidation rules whenever external actions alter environment state. The host runtime owns assembly, token budgets, records, and execution gates. Selection and compaction can use heuristics or model-generated candidates, which the runtime must check against the task's requirements and retained evidence before admission.

The chapter follows the repair agent through its next decision, and each section answers the question the previous one leaves open. The runtime first decides which evidence the next step needs and how the input allowance divides among competing roles (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision). Admitting that evidence does not mean the model can use it, so @sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics separates the window an interface accepts from the context a model reliably acts on. The selected items then need a layout that keeps their sources distinct and their stable prefix reusable across turns (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging). When history outgrows the budget, compaction (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction) and audited progress records (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-summarization) shorten it without erasing causal evidence or refuted hypotheses. When the agent's own edits change the workspace, invalidation (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot) withdraws the observations that no longer describe it. Evaluation (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation) then asks how to show that a complete policy lowers the cost per accepted task.

## The Working-Set Decision {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision}

As our connection-pool investigation unfolds, the runtime accumulates far more information than was present at initialization. A controlled test has shown that a connection returned to the pool while a waiting client remained blocked, so the initial timeout hypothesis has lost support and missed notification is now the leading candidate explanation. The next model call must build on these findings. If the runtime replays the entire conversational history without distinguishing raw observations from superseded hypotheses, it forces the model to weigh discounted failure modes alongside the evidence that disproved them.

Consider the codebase at version `r17`, where the relevant files are `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py`, and the failure is captured by the reproducer `test_waiter_notified_on_return`. Before prompting the model for a candidate patch, the runtime must decide which source excerpts, test results, interface constraints, and open questions belong in the upcoming prompt. This choice is the **working-set decision**\index{Working-set decision!definition}\index{Context engineering!working-set decision}, the runtime's selection of the bounded subset of task information needed to run the next concrete step. Making that choice is the first obligation of treating context as a selected working set (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}).

The term draws on Denning's classic working-set model of program behavior [@denning1968].\index{Working set!Denning model} Over any time window, a running program references only a fraction of its total address space, so an operating system avoids thrashing by keeping those active pages in physical memory while leaving dormant pages on backing storage. An agent runtime faces a similar residency problem when it stages tokens in context to support the next step without exhausting its prompt budget, yet one structural difference separates context engineering from virtual memory. Denning's working set is measured from page references the program has already issued, whereas an agent runtime must assemble the context working set *before* calling the model, predicting what the upcoming decision will need.[^fn-belady-optimal-replacement] Moreover, standard foundation model interfaces report only generated tokens and emit no hardware-style reference bits to show which staged context tokens the model actually relied on during inference.

[^fn-belady-optimal-replacement]: **Optimal Replacement (MIN)**: @belady1966study evaluated page-replacement algorithms against an optimal offline baseline that evicts the page whose next reference lies farthest in the future. Practical operating systems approximate this unattainable ideal using historical access patterns such as least recently used (LRU). An agent context runtime lacks even that access history. The model interface reports no reference bits for the tokens it processes, so working-set selection must rely on explicit domain heuristics and structured task state rather than on observed cache reuse. \index{Belady optimal replacement!context selection}

In context management, relevance to the next step must govern selection rather than chronological recency. Core user constraints set at the start of a session remain binding after dozens of intermediate tool calls, whereas a lengthy test log produced moments ago may contribute only a single exit code. Candidate information also comes from well beyond the dialogue history: system instructions, tool declarations, newly read source files, and retrieved reference documents [@lewis2020retrieval] all compete for space in the assembled request. The runtime must build a working representation from these sources without letting any staged copy outrank its origin, because authority stays with the source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). The environment remains the only authority on system state, and runtime policy, not the model, decides which actions are permitted.

To organize this selection, the runtime builds a **context manifest**\index{Context manifest!definition}, a structured inventory that lists each item chosen for the upcoming request and why the next step needs it. The manifest for the connection-pool repair's next request (@tbl-vol3-context-manifest) reads like a specification rather than a raw byte stream, naming each entry and the exact content it supplies. Code snippets and test logs keep their source and version labels, and their contents enter the prompt only where the next decision requires them.

| Selected entry          | Content needed for the next step                                                                                                                                            |
|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Goal and constraints    | Repair waiter notification; preserve the public API; remain within the approved workspace; do not deploy to production.                                                     |
| Current artifacts       | Relevant source and test excerpts from `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` at `r17`, together with the configuration used by the controlled test.                        |
| Observed result         | On `r17`, the controlled waiter/return test recorded an available connection while a waiter remained blocked. Keep the test identity and conditions attached to the result. |
| Hypothesis status       | The timeout explanation has lost support. Missed notification remains a hypothesis, not an established cause.                                                               |
| Repair and check status | No candidate patch has yet been checked. Behavior outside the controlled reproducer remains unresolved.                                                                     |
| Next bounded step       | Propose a candidate change to the notification path using the current excerpts; do not report the defect as repaired.                                                       |

: **Selecting the next request**: Each entry supplies a distinct part of the illustrative connection-pool decision. Version labels identify the example’s artifacts, not measured repository revisions. {#tbl-vol3-context-manifest tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Building this manifest requires careful filtering. Keeping a failure log without tying it to its source commit (`r17`) can mislead later turns into reading an old error trace as evidence against a newly patched file. Likewise, recording a short label like "notification bug" without noting its uncertainty turns a working hypothesis into a settled root cause. Conversely, keeping the full dialogue of rejected theories wastes space once the runtime records which test refuted the timeout hypothesis. While a foundation model can help summarize earlier turns to draft this manifest, the runtime must check those candidate summaries against recorded environment observations before admitting them into the prompt.

The active working context must also stay separate from durable records in external storage. Rather than inlining a long test log into the prompt, the runtime can supply a **raw-payload handle**\index{Raw-payload handle!definition}, a short reference to an external record that an authorized tool can read on demand under access and retention rules. This design enforces the **handle rule**\index{Handle rule!definition}: once a payload moves behind a handle, it re-enters the working context only through an explicit, checked read. If a later step needs a specific stack-trace line or configuration value omitted from the initial prompt, the model calls a retrieval tool to bring that slice into context.

Every working-set candidate must fit within the endpoint's context admission bounds. When an endpoint shares one context window across inputs and outputs, the serialized prompt length $\SequenceLength$ must satisfy $\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit$, where $\OutputLimit$ is the token budget reserved for generation. When providers enforce separate input and output limits, $\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow$ applies directly. The runtime must count tokens on the fully formatted wire request (system envelopes, chat delimiters, and JSON tool schemas included) rather than summing isolated strings, because tokenizer merges and framing overhead can easily erase the savings of a shorter evidence block.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The admission bound and the output headroom $\OutputLimit$ it reserves are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-output-headroom.
:::

While this inequality sets the overall ceiling, the runtime must divide the available input space across the four roles in the manifest:

$$
\SystemInstructionTokenCount + \ToolDeclarationTokenCount + \TaskStateTokenCount + \ObservationTokenCount \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit.
$$ {#eq-vol3-context-budget-partition}

Here $\SystemInstructionTokenCount$ counts the static system instructions, $\ToolDeclarationTokenCount$ counts API schemas and tool declarations, $\TaskStateTokenCount$ counts active constraints, progress records, and staged source or test excerpts, and $\ObservationTokenCount$ counts recent tool outputs and user steering. Because all four terms share a fixed ceiling, growth in any one term squeezes the others. A runtime that appends every raw tool output[^fn-react-appended-observations] lets $\ObservationTokenCount$ grow on every turn until command-line logs crowd out $\TaskStateTokenCount$, the constraints and code excerpts the next decision needs. Whereas appending lets observations expand until they displace task state, selection holds each role's share steady by moving older results into external records that a handle can still reach (@fig-vol3-working-set-selection).

[^fn-react-appended-observations]: **Interleaved Observations**: ReAct prompting interleaves reasoning traces, tool actions, and observation payloads within an ever-expanding prompt transcript [@yao2023react]. While keeping full execution history visible simplifies early prototyping, it carries a steep cost, because the unchecked growth of $\ObservationTokenCount$ consumes prompt capacity and raises input token costs on every subsequent call. \index{ReAct!appended observations}

@Eq-vol3-context-budget-partition is a planning budget rather than an exact identity, because sub-word tokenization across joined strings does not equal the sum of separately tokenized parts. The runtime must therefore check the assembled wire request against the provider's limit, and when the request runs over, the budget partition tells the runtime which share (usually the observation buffer or older history) to trim or compact first. Prompt staging (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging) then orders these same four components by how often they change so the serving engine can reuse their cached prefix.

::: {#fig-vol3-working-set-selection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Selection Protects the State Budget**: Each bar is one serialized request, stacked by the four terms of @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition beneath the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ hatched above it. Appending every tool result (A) lets $\ObservationTokenCount$ grow until it displaces the task state the next decision needs. Selection (B) keeps each term's share by moving older results into retained records outside the request, where a handle can reach them if a later decision needs them. Segment heights are schematic, not measured token counts." fig-alt="Two panels of stacked vertical bars for turns t, t plus 1, and t plus 2, on a shared scale with a dashed input limit S max minus K max and a hatched output reserve up to S max. Each bar stacks gray system and tools segments, a green state segment, and amber observation slices, one slice per tool result. In panel A, append every result, the bars hold two, four, and six slices and the state segment shrinks until it turns red at turn t plus 2, labeled state squeezed. In panel B, select for the next step, all three bars hold two slices and an unchanged state segment, labeled state keeps its share; an arrow moves older slices into a violet retained-records stack of four slices outside the bars, and a dashed arrow labeled retrieve by handle returns to the last bar."}
![](images/svg/context_working_set_dynamics.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-usable-context-budget
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EVIDENCE BUDGET OF A REPAIR REQUEST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition; nbk-04-evidence-budget.
# │ Goal: Show how many appended turns fit before observations overflow.
# │ Show: Evidence share, turns that fit, per-turn digest for the full horizon,
# │       and the input bill of appending vs. selecting over the horizon.
# │ How: Registry window and step budget; scenario sizes for the four terms.
# │ Note: Scenario token counts are serialized-request stipulations, not
# │       measurements of any product; bills assume no prefix reuse.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class UsableContextBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    scenario = Scenarios.RepairContextBudget  # registry window and step budget; scenario role sizes
    window = scenario.window
    horizon = scenario.turns
    output_reserve = scenario.output_reserve
    system_tokens = scenario.system_tokens
    tool_tokens = scenario.tool_tokens
    state_tokens = scenario.state_tokens
    obs_per_turn = scenario.observation_per_turn
    obs_digest = scenario.digest_tokens
    obs_selected = scenario.selected_observation

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    r = scenario.result
    input_limit = r.input_limit
    evidence = r.evidence_tokens
    evidence_share = r.evidence_share
    obs_budget = r.observation_budget
    turns_fit = r.turns_fit
    turns_fit_half = r.digest_turns
    digest_max = r.max_observation_per_turn
    fixed = r.fixed_tokens
    append_bill = r.append_bill
    select_bill = r.select_bill
    bill_ratio = r.bill_ratio
    window_needed = r.final_append_with_reserve

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(turns_fit < horizon <= turns_fit_half, "Appending overflows inside the step budget; halving fits it")
    check(fixed + obs_selected <= input_limit, "The selecting policy fits every turn")
    check(window_needed > window, "The appending policy's last request exceeds the window")
    check(1.5 < bill_ratio < 3, "Appending bills roughly twice the selected input")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    window_str = fmt_int(window)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    reserve_str = fmt_int(output_reserve)
    system_str = fmt_int(system_tokens)
    tool_str = fmt_int(tool_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_int(state_tokens)
    obs_str = fmt_int(obs_per_turn)
    obs_half_str = fmt_int(obs_digest)
    obs_selected_str = fmt_int(obs_selected)
    input_limit_str = fmt_int(input_limit)
    evidence_str = fmt_int(evidence)
    evidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(evidence_share, style="prose", precision=1)
    obs_budget_str = fmt_int(obs_budget)
    turns_fit_str = fmt_int(turns_fit)
    overflow_turn_str = fmt_int(r.overflow_turn)
    turns_fit_half_str = fmt_int(turns_fit_half)
    digest_max_str = fmt_int(digest_max)
    append_bill_str = fmt_int(append_bill)
    select_bill_str = fmt_int(select_bill)
    bill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bill_ratio, precision=1)
    window_needed_str = fmt_int(window_needed)
```

::: {#nbk-04-evidence-budget .callout-notebook title="How much of the window is evidence"}

**Problem**: In our reference repository-repair harness, an agent runs inside a `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token context window under a `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget. The runtime reserves `{python} UsableContextBudget.reserve_str` tokens for generation ($\OutputLimit$) and assigns `{python} UsableContextBudget.system_str` tokens to system instructions ($\SystemInstructionTokenCount$) and `{python} UsableContextBudget.tool_str` tokens to tool declarations ($\ToolDeclarationTokenCount$). Dynamic task state (constraints, progress records, and active code excerpts) takes `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens ($\TaskStateTokenCount$). If every raw tool result is appended directly at `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_str` tokens per turn, how many turns fit within the window, and what maximum per-turn observation size lets the agent finish the full step budget?

**Variables**: The context window and step horizon come from the registry's repository-repair harness profile, while component sizes and per-turn observation counts are scenario values for fully serialized wire requests.

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition, the usable input allowance is `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str` − `{python} UsableContextBudget.reserve_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.input_limit_str` tokens. Subtracting system instructions and tool declarations leaves `{python} UsableContextBudget.evidence_str` tokens (`{python} UsableContextBudget.evidence_pct_str` of the context window) for state and observations, and deducting the `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens of state leaves an observation budget of `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` tokens. Under naive appending, this budget holds `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` / `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_str` turns. Lasting all `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str` turns requires keeping the per-turn observation payload to at most `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` / `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.digest_max_str` tokens.

**Result**: The appending policy overflows the context window at turn `{python} UsableContextBudget.overflow_turn_str`, well short of the `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn budget.

**Systems insight**: Because the number of feasible turns equals the observation budget divided by the per-turn observation size, observation volume is the primary design lever. Compacting each result into an informative `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_half_str`-token digest extends the run to `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_half_str` turns and clears the step budget. Fitting inside the window, however, is only the first cost. Because an appending policy re-reads every accumulated token on each call, its cumulative input bill grows quadratically in $\TurnHorizon$. This follows the re-send pattern of @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend with a per-turn append $\TurnAppendLength$ of `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_str` tokens, where the first request already holds one tool result, so the appended sum runs to $\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2$. Selection keeps the bill linear. Across this step budget, and even granting the appending policy a window large enough to admit its final request, appending bills `{python} UsableContextBudget.append_bill_str` input tokens against `{python} UsableContextBudget.select_bill_str` for selection, `{python} UsableContextBudget.bill_mult_str` as many. That extra spend enters the numerator of $\CostPerAcceptedTask$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task) on every attempt.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/ch04_append_select_bill.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two curves of cumulative input bill, in tokens, from turn 1 to turn 30. A red curve labeled append bends upward; a blue line labeled select rises straight. A bracket at turn 30 spans the gap between them, labeled 2.1 times."}

*Appending re-reads every result, so its bill bends upward; selection stays linear.*
:::

The notebooks throughout this chapter reuse this baseline scenario, adopting the `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token window, the `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget, and the component token allocations defined above. Whereas the repair agent binds on the growth of $\ObservationTokenCount$ against $\TaskStateTokenCount$, the other three lighthouses stress different terms of the same partition.

::: {#lhs-04-context-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Context by archetype"}

```{=latex}
\begin{minipage}{1\linewidth}
```
Each recurring workload places pressure on a distinct component of the context budget in @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition, calling for a different runtime mechanism (@tbl-vol3-context-by-archetype).

| **Lighthouse**        | **What fills the request**                                                                                                                                | **Binding constraint**                                                                        | **Mechanism that answers it**                                                                                                                      |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Repair agent**      | Source excerpts, test logs, and a progress record from its own workspace, accumulating over a `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget | Growth of $\ObservationTokenCount$ displacing $\TaskStateTokenCount$                          | Compaction and progress records (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction)                                                                         |
| **Research agent**    | Retrieved pages and search results written by third parties                                                                                               | Third-party text that dominates $\ObservationTokenCount$ and may carry instructions           | Staging that keeps each span's source attached (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-source-scope); enforcement in @sec-vol3-security-quarantined-readers |
| **Remediation agent** | Readings of shared production state that other actors change                                                                                              | Staleness between the read and the action                                                     | Invalidation and action-time preconditions (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot)                                                             |
| **Support agent**     | Fixed policy instructions and tool declarations, one customer record, a short session                                                                     | $\SystemInstructionTokenCount+\ToolDeclarationTokenCount$ repeated across many short sessions | A stable leading block of instructions and declarations that later calls reuse (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-exact-prefix)                        |

: **Context by archetype**: The four recurring workloads bind on different terms of the same input budget. {#tbl-vol3-context-by-archetype tbl-colwidths="[16,34,25,25]"}

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}
```

**Systems insight**: The same budget equation binds on different constraints across workloads: token growth for the repair agent, source tracking for the research agent, freshness for the remediation agent, and prefix reuse across short sessions for the support agent. As a result, a policy tuned for one workload rarely transfers directly to another. Compaction rules that keep a repair agent within its token budget do not solve the main risk of a research agent, where untrusted external text matters far more than transcript length.

:::

Every one of these budgets governs *admission*, ensuring that a serialized payload fits inside the provider's context limit, yet admission alone does not mean the prompt supports the next decision. A prompt can obey the budget while omitting the return path needed to write a patch, or it can include every relevant code excerpt while burying version boundaries under old error logs. Sizing a context budget is therefore only the first step; the runtime must also ask how well the model can find and use the tokens admitted into that window.

## Usable Working Context {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics}

In notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}, the `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token window admits the investigation's full transcript for its first `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_str` turns, yet fitting an entire history inside the window does not mean the runtime should send all of it. What matters is what each item contributes to the pending decision: an omitted synchronization contract can ruin a proposed repair, whereas ten pages of repeated timeout speculation only add noise. Raw request length cannot separate essential evidence from distraction.

The **nominal context capacity**\index{Nominal context capacity!definition} is the maximum sequence length that the configured model interface accepts under its input and generation limits. How well the model reasons over a chosen set of instructions and evidence is a separate question, answered only by testing concrete tasks against explicit quality criteria (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set})\index{Principle!context is a selected working set}.

::: {#dfn-usable-working-context .callout-definition title="Usable working context"}

***Usable working context***\index{Usable working context!definition} is the context content, organization, and length with which a specified model and invocation configuration meet a chosen quality criterion on a stated workload.

1. **Significance**: Usable working context, rather than the nominal window, determines how much of the input allowance $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$ effectively supports decisions. It dictates how many turns an execution trajectory can sustain before selection or compaction must intervene, directly setting the input token cost per accepted task in $\CostPerAcceptedTask$.
2. **Distinction**: Nominal capacity is an architectural boundary of the serving interface that admits a request; usable working context is an empirical property of a task, model, and representation that only evaluation can establish.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a fixed fraction of the nominal window, or success on an isolated synthetic retrieval probe, as a universal guarantee of usable context for a production workload.

:::

For a software repair workload, that criterion might require candidate patches to pass designated regression tests while staying within a permitted edit scope, whereas an information extraction workload requires high precision and recall against a target schema. Because failure modes differ across workloads, usable working context must be measured on each workload rather than read off the model card.

### Testing usable working context {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-usable-context-test}

Testing whether a context length is usable starts with what the task asks the model to do with the staged text. A model that scores nearly perfectly on an isolated retrieval probe[^fn-needle-haystack-probe] by finding a single planted fact in a long input can still fail a repair decision at the same length. The repair requires relating observed symptoms to source files, honoring API invariants, and separating a measured failure from an unverified hypothesis (@tbl-vol3-capacity-comparison). Synthetic retrieval probes quickly flag gross blind spots, but validating a context policy requires testing actual task decisions under realistic conditions.

[^fn-needle-haystack-probe]: **Needle-in-a-Haystack Probes**: The best-known isolated retrieval probe plants a short fact, the needle, in long distractor text and asks the model to return it. @hsieh2024ruler found that models scoring nearly perfectly on this probe degraded sharply as length grew on tasks that require multi-hop tracing and aggregation, and that only about half of the models tested held satisfactory performance at the context length all of them claimed to support. The gap between the probe and the harder tasks is the gap between nominal capacity and usable working context. \index{Needle-in-a-haystack!usable context}

| Test obligation           | Isolated key-retrieval probe                        | Connection-pool repair decision                                                                               |
|:--------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Identify relevant content | Return the requested planted value.                 | Find the source, test conditions, and observation relevant to the notification path.                          |
| Interpret relationships   | Match the queried key to its value.                 | Tie the failure to `r17` and distinguish the missed-notification hypothesis from the observed blocked waiter. |
| Respect task constraints  | Meet the probe’s answer requirements.               | Propose a scoped change while preserving the public API and leaving untested behavior unresolved.             |
| Establish success         | Compare the returned value with the probe’s target. | Apply the chosen candidate checks and scope criteria; report only what they establish.                        |

: **Retrieval and decision scope**: A simple retrieval probe and the running repair example test different capabilities. {#tbl-vol3-capacity-comparison tbl-colwidths="[23,29,48]"}

Context organization directly affects task success even when all required facts are present in the prompt. Evaluating multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, @liu2024lost reported marked sensitivity to the position of relevant information across model architectures, with accuracy dropping substantially when key facts appeared in the middle of the input. This position sensitivity, known as **lost in the middle**\index{Lost in the middle!definition}, means systems engineers cannot treat context as an unordered bag of tokens. Placement policies must be tested on the target workload, because how accuracy varies with position depends on the model family and prompt layout.

Length degrades comprehension even when every required fact remains in the input. One long-context benchmark isolates that effect by rewriting each of its stories at lengths from a few hundred tokens to the full text while preserving the details its questions depend on. A change in score across lengths therefore reflects the surrounding material rather than missing evidence [@fictionlive2025bench]. Answering requires following the order of events and drawing inferences from implicitly stated information, a task closer to a repair decision than to returning a planted value. @Fig-vol3-context-length-comprehension plots the scores against the length of story in context, as aggregated by @epochai2026benchmarks.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-context-length-comprehension
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMPREHENSION VS. CONTEXT LENGTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-context-length-comprehension and the paragraph after it.
# │ Goal: Quantify how far comprehension falls as the same story lengthens.
# │ Show: Median score at the shortest version, at 8K and 60K tokens; how
# │       many models hold 90% at 60K.
# │ How:  Literature.LongContextComprehension, models scored at every
# │       length through 60K tokens.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class ContextLengthComprehension:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    scenario = Scenarios.FictionLiveBenchThrough60K  # Literature.LongContextComprehension
    questions = 36  # questions per length, from the benchmark methodology
    hold_bar = scenario.hold_bar

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    r = scenario.result
    n_scored = r.scored_models
    median_short = r.median["0"]
    median_8k = round(r.median["8k"], 2)  # whole percent: 36 questions per cell
    median_60k = round(r.median["60k"], 2)
    n_hold = r.held_count
    lo_60k = r.lowest_last
    hi_60k = r.highest_last

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(median_short > median_8k >= median_60k, "Prose says the median falls with length")
    check(n_hold < n_scored / 10, "Prose says only a few models hold 90% at 60K")
    check(median_short - median_60k > 1 / 3, "Caption says the median model loses more than a third by 60K")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_scored_str = fmt_int(n_scored)
    n_hold_str = fmt_int(n_hold)
    questions_str = fmt_int(questions)
    median_short_str = fmt_percent(median_short, style="prose")
    median_8k_str = fmt_percent(median_8k, precision=0, style="prose")
    median_60k_str = fmt_percent(median_60k, precision=0, style="prose")
    hold_bar_str = fmt_percent(hold_bar, style="prose")
    lo_60k_str = fmt_int(round(100 * lo_60k))
    hi_60k_str = fmt_percent(round(hi_60k, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
```

:::: {#fig-vol3-context-length-comprehension fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Comprehension Falls with Context Length**: Accuracy on the same stories as the version placed in context grows from the shortest rewrite to 192K tokens. The shaded band spans the middle half of the `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.n_scored_str` models scored at every length through 60K tokens; colored lines trace six individual models. A few models stay near the top at every length, while the median model loses more than a third of its accuracy by 60K tokens. Each point rests on `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.questions_str` questions, so single-length wiggles are within sampling noise. Data from @fictionlive2025bench via @epochai2026benchmarks." fig-alt="Line chart of comprehension accuracy from 0 to 100 percent against story length placed in context, with eleven categories from 0 to 192k tokens. A gray band falls from near 100 percent at 0 tokens to roughly between 40 and 70 percent at 60k. Three colored lines stay between about 80 and 100 percent across all lengths. One orange line falls to about 50 percent, and two lines fall below 40 percent by 8k tokens and stop at 60k. A legend below the chart names the band and six models."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMPREHENSION VS. CONTEXT LENGTH (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-context-length-comprehension
# │
# │ Goal: Show comprehension degrading with context length, and how much
# │       models differ at the same length.
# │ Show: Interquartile band over fully scored models; six model traces.
# │ How: Literature.LongContextComprehension (MLSysIM); book_style.setup_plot().
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import Literature, Scenarios
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.4))

# ┌── 1. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
entries = Literature.LongContextComprehension.entries
lengths = ["0", "400", "1k", "2k", "4k", "8k", "16k", "32k", "60k", "120k", "192k"]
x = np.arange(len(lengths))
sweep = Scenarios.FictionLiveBenchThrough60K.result  # models scored at every length through 60k
band_lengths = sweep.lengths
traces = [
    ("gpt-5-2025-08-07_medium", "GPT-5 (medium)", "BlueLine", "o"),
    ("grok-4-0709", "Grok 4", "VioletLine", "s"),
    ("kimi-k2.5", "Kimi K2.5", "GreenLine", "^"),
    ("deepinfra/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct", "Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B", "OrangeLine", "D"),
    ("chutes/gpt-oss-120b", "gpt-oss-120b", "BrownLine", "v"),
    ("nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2", "Nemotron Nano 9B v2", "RedLine", "P"),
]

# ┌── 2. RENDER ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.fill_between(
    x[: len(band_lengths)],
    [100 * sweep.q25[n] for n in band_lengths],
    [100 * sweep.q75[n] for n in band_lengths],
    color=COLORS["grid"],
    alpha=0.35,
    lw=0,
    label=f"Middle half of {sweep.scored_models} models",
)
for key, label, color, marker in traces:
    row = next(e for e in entries if e["model"] == key)
    y = np.array([row["score_" + n] if row["score_" + n] is not None else np.nan for n in lengths]) * 100
    ok = ~np.isnan(y)
    ax.plot(x[ok], y[ok], "-", marker=marker, color=COLORS[color], ms=4, lw=1.6, label=label)

# ┌── 3. DECORATE ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(lengths)
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)
ax.set_xlabel("Story length placed in context (tokens)")

ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.15), ncol=4)
```

::::

Two features of @fig-vol3-context-length-comprehension bear directly on the working budget: the decline starts early and runs deep, and models differ widely at any fixed length. Across the `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.n_scored_str` fully scored models, the median falls from `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.median_short_str` on the shortest version to `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.median_8k_str` at 8K tokens and `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.median_60k_str` at 60K, with only `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.n_hold_str` models staying at or above `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.hold_bar_str` at 60K. At 60K tokens, scores also span from `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.lo_60k_str` to `{python} ContextLengthComprehension.hi_60k_str`. This spread is the empirical content of the definition above. Usable working context belongs to a specified model, configuration, and workload, so the budget must be found by evaluation rather than read from the window.

A first-order mechanism explains why appending distractor tokens cannot be treated as free. Within an individual attention head, a query assigns weight to each visible key through a softmax operation [@vaswani2017]. For a target key with scaled logit $\TargetKeyLogit$ alongside $\CompetingKeyCount$ other keys with logits $\CompetingKeyLogit_j = \QueryVector\cdot\KeyVector_j/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}$ for head dimension $\AttentionHeadDimension$, the target's weight is

$$
\TargetKeyAttentionWeight = \frac{e^{\TargetKeyLogit}}{e^{\TargetKeyLogit} + \sum_{j=1}^{\CompetingKeyCount} e^{\CompetingKeyLogit_j}}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-softmax-dilution}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-softmax-dilution
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED-NORMALIZER DILUTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-softmax-dilution, working set capacity section.
# │ Goal: Show how fixed-logit background keys shrink one target's weight.
# │ Show: Target attention weight at two context lengths.
# │ How: Toy logits held fixed; only the number of background keys changes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class SoftmaxDilution:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    scenario = Scenarios.ToyHeadAttentionDilution  # toy logits held fixed
    z_target = int(scenario.target_logit)  # toy scaled logit for the target key
    z_background = int(scenario.background_logit)  # toy scaled logit for every other key
    short_len = scenario.short_keys  # total keys, short context
    long_len = scenario.long_keys  # total keys, long context

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_short = scenario.result.short_weight
    alpha_long = scenario.result.long_weight

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < alpha_long < alpha_short < 1, "More fixed-logit keys lower the target weight")
    check(alpha_short > 0.9 and alpha_long < 0.05, "Toy endpoints show the stated contrast")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    z_target_str = fmt_int(z_target)
    z_background_str = fmt_int(z_background)
    short_len_str = fmt_int(short_len)
    long_len_str = fmt_int(long_len)
    alpha_short_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha_short, style="prose", precision=1)
    alpha_long_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha_long, style="prose", precision=1)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_working_sets_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Line chart of target attention weight from 0 to 100 percent against the number of keys, from few to many on a log scale. The curve starts near 100 percent at a green dot and falls to near zero at a red dot."}

*Fixed-logit distractors shrink the target's share of one normalizer.*
:::

All weights share a single normalizer. Because each additional key contributes a strictly positive term $e^{\CompetingKeyLogit_j}$ to the denominator of @eq-vol3-softmax-dilution, expanding the sequence length while holding logits constant depresses the target key's share of attention. This structural decay is **attention dilution**\index{Attention dilution!definition}. In a toy head with a target logit of `{python} SoftmaxDilution.z_target_str` and every background logit at `{python} SoftmaxDilution.z_background_str`, the target commands `{python} SoftmaxDilution.alpha_short_pct_str` of the weight among `{python} SoftmaxDilution.short_len_str` keys. When the context expands to `{python} SoftmaxDilution.long_len_str` keys, that same target's share falls to `{python} SoftmaxDilution.alpha_long_pct_str`, even though no single background key is individually competitive.

In agent execution, this effect is often worse than unrelated filler would produce.[^fn-irrelevant-context-distraction] Stale tool outputs, superseded logs, and earlier source reads share identifiers such as `waiter`, `connection`, and `timeout` with the evidence that matters, so they produce large inner products with query vectors and keep elevated logits. This dynamic is a sufficient condition for dilution under fixed logits, not a deterministic forecast of failure. Production models sharpen logits, route evidence across multiple attention heads and layers, and learn position-dependent retrieval behaviors, which is why @liu2024lost measured degradation empirically rather than deriving it analytically. Trained models also show a second consequence of the shared normalizer. Because the weights must sum to one, a query with no strong match deposits its leftover weight on the first few positions, which act as attention sinks regardless of their content [@xiao2024streamingllm]. Sinks change where leftover weight goes, not the dilution argument, and every staged token still adds a term to the normalizer that the evidence for the next decision must compete against.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Why cache eviction policies must retain attention-sink tokens is developed in @sec-vol3-kvcache-intrasequence.
:::

[^fn-irrelevant-context-distraction]: **Distracting Context**: @shi2023distracted added irrelevant sentences to grade-school arithmetic problems and found that model accuracy fell dramatically, although the added text changed nothing about the answer. Because the distractors were irrelevant by construction, the drop measures interference rather than missing information. That interference is the cost an agent pays for every superseded log line and stale file read it keeps in the request. \index{Irrelevant context!accuracy loss}

### Choosing a working budget {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-working-budget}

Sizing a working budget from the window's admission bound alone can still leave a request too long for the model to use reliably. Choosing a working budget therefore takes two steps, and only the first can be computed from the window. In notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}, the admission bound leaves `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` tokens for observations in any one request. An appending policy must hold each result to `{python} UsableContextBudget.digest_max_str` tokens to last all `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str` turns, whereas a selecting policy can spend up to that whole share on every request because it does not accumulate. The ceiling says what fits, not what the next decision can use, so the second step searches beneath it empirically.

To find that working point, engineers test complete context policies on representative task suites (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation) and choose the budget that meets the workload's quality criterion at the lowest effective cost. Because a context policy sets a token limit alongside what material is retrieved, how structured data is formatted, and where each piece sits in the prompt, decision quality must be weighed alongside input size, latency, and token spend. Additional context can supply needed grounding, add harmless noise, or degrade reasoning through dilution, which means the quality curve is rarely monotonic and seldom has a single sharp peak. A documented operating envelope must therefore name the workload, model configuration, quality threshold, and test conditions.

These choices carry direct resource consequences under model-call cost accounting. Uncached tokens add prefill latency and compute charges, whereas aligned prefix caching spreads prompt costs across repeated turns. High cache hit rates or discounted per-token prices mean little if stale context hurts decisions, yet pruning context too sharply to save prefill cost can strip away required constraints. The engineering goal is to meet the task quality bar at the lowest effective cost per accepted task, $\CostPerAcceptedTask$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Trimming unneeded tokens lowers the attempt cost in the numerator, whereas dropping a needed fact lowers the acceptance probability $\AcceptanceProbability$ in the denominator and drives up total spend across failed runs.

In the connection-pool repair example, keeping the full transcript of early exploratory turns wastes space once distilled test observations, code snippets, interface invariants, and active hypotheses are ready to guide the next patch. Stripping away a required interface contract or error log merely to fit an arbitrary sub-budget, however, is just as harmful. When no candidate policy meets both the task criterion and the available budget, the runtime must fetch the missing information, narrow the scope of the next permitted action, or report the limit. Passing a request-admission check never certifies that the staged context is adequate. Once the runtime selects that working set and bounds its token budget, it must arrange those items into a concrete prompt layout that keeps sources and evidence relationships distinct while separating stable prefix content from turn-by-turn updates.

## Staging the Next Invocation {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging}

In our connection-pool repair task, the selected manifest holds several distinct kinds of material: public API constraints, source excerpts from `src/pool.py` at revision `r17`, test results from `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, and the missed-notification working hypothesis alongside an abandoned timeout explanation. Concatenating these items into a flat, unlabeled string would blur the distinctions that guide the model's next decision. Once a selection policy chooses the working set for an upcoming call, staging turns those entries into a structured request payload. That assembly step records the source, authority, and revision of every item so the model can tell policy instructions apart from test observations and working hypotheses, while ordering the content to minimize token churn across consecutive calls.

### Ordering by change rate {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-change-rate-ordering}

Minimizing token churn across calls means ordering the prompt by how often each piece of context changes, placing stable material ahead of volatile updates. This layout partitions the serialized prompt into three regions: the **root**, the **trunk**, and the **leaf**\index{Context zone!definition}, which group content strictly by its update cadence during a trajectory rather than by message role or authority (@tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification). In the repair scenario from notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}, the root holds `{python} UsableContextBudget.system_str` tokens of system instructions and `{python} UsableContextBudget.tool_str` tokens of tool declarations. The trunk holds `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens of evolving task state, and the leaf receives `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_selected_str` tokens of newly staged observations.

| Zone  | Contents in the repair request                                                                                           | When it changes                                                                       |
|:------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Root  | Application instructions and available tool definitions                                                                  | The application contract or tool interface changes                                    |
| Trunk | Task constraints, the current progress record, and selected source and test content at `r17`                             | A task constraint changes, an artifact is edited, or the progress record is refreshed |
| Leaf  | The latest scoped test observation and the next bounded step, here proposing a candidate change to the notification path | New evidence or a new next-step decision arrives                                      |

: **Context ordered by change rate**: The zones help preserve a stable request prefix. Message roles and source metadata remain separate from these placement choices. {#tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification}

Prefix stability must never override correctness. The root stays fixed only while its declarations remain accurate; if a tool definition changes during a session, the runtime updates the root on the next call and accepts the cache miss. Likewise, when a candidate patch advances the repository from `r17` to `r18`, the runtime cannot keep `r17` source code in the trunk just to keep the prefix warm. The earlier test failure remains valid historical evidence about `r17`, but checking whether it persists on the patched workspace requires a fresh run (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot).

Information can also move between zones as a trajectory advances. An observation first staged in the leaf can fold into the trunk's progress record during a scheduled refresh so long as its source, version, and scope stay attached. Conversely, a per-step instruction injected into the leaf keeps its full authority despite sitting at the end of the prompt. Zone placement sets the physical order of tokens to match their change rate, whereas schemas and message roles carry provenance and meaning.

### Preserving source and scope {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-source-scope}

As observations move from the leaf into the trunk or across compaction passes, each entry must keep the revision and execution conditions that produced it so the model does not read a local result as a universal fact about the codebase. For our failing test case, the host runtime attaches the test name, the workspace revision (`r17`), the test configuration, and a run identifier directly to the observation payload. This discipline enforces the **scope rule**\index{Scope rule!definition}:[^fn-why-where-provenance] an observation supports claims only for the artifact versions and execution conditions under which it was gathered, and every later context transformation (summarization, compaction, and invalidation alike) must preserve those bounds.

[^fn-why-where-provenance]: **Why- and Where-Provenance**: Database research distinguishes why-provenance, the source records that justify a result's existence, from where-provenance, the source locations its values were copied from [@buneman2001why]. The scope rule demands both for every observation: which execution and artifact versions justify its existence, and which payload spans supplied its values. A result that loses either becomes an unattributed claim that later compaction can silently generalize. \index{Provenance!scope rule}

The runtime builds this framing on the outside rather than reading it from text inside the observation. A serializer places raw tool output strictly as a literal data value inside a structured envelope so that mismatched quotes, markdown delimiters, or control characters cannot corrupt the surrounding schema. Even with that framing, the payload itself remains an **untrusted span**\index{Untrusted span!definition}: arbitrary text whose arrival the runtime can record, but whose claims it cannot vouch for. In a traditional parser, escaping quotes keeps a string literal out of the executable syntax tree. A language model, by contrast, processes the framing tags and the escaped data string inside them as one sequence of tokens in the same attention pass. Careful encoding therefore stops format injection at the host serializer, yet it cannot stop the model from attending to and following adversarial instructions hidden inside the text [@greshake2023not].

Provenance labels therefore guide interpretation rather than enforcing security. Marking a tool output as untrusted data helps the model weigh its source, but if an observation tells the agent to drop a database or overwrite production credentials, the model may still propose that call. Security boundaries (filesystem sandboxes, read-only mounts, and deployment blocks) must run in host code outside the model's prompt interpretation: staging keeps instructions and observations distinct in the request, while host gates enforce what may run.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The host-side information-flow policy that limits what untrusted context may influence and where private data may flow is enforced in @sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking.
:::

How much weight this distinction carries depends on the workload. The repair agent's observations come mostly from its own workspace, whose files change only when the agent or its tests change them. The research agent fills its requests with third-party text, so its $\ObservationTokenCount$ consists mostly of untrusted spans (lighthouse \ref{lhs-04-context-by-archetype}). For that workload the untrusted-span boundary, not token growth, is the binding concern. Once each entry's source and scope are framed, the serializer must emit the root and trunk in a repeatable token sequence so the serving engine can reuse their cached attention state.

### Preserving an exact prefix {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-exact-prefix}

Because causal self-attention computes each token's keys and values from all preceding tokens, a single changed token near the beginning of a request invalidates the cached key-value (KV) attention state for every later position, even when thousands of trailing tokens are identical. Serving engines equipped with prefix caching[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse] skip redundant prefill computation only across an identical leading token sequence, because attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). Ordering the zones by change rate is what turns this rule into savings. A call that changes only the leaf reuses the root and trunk, whereas a compaction that rewrites the trunk ends reuse at the root boundary and forces recomputation of every later token (@fig-vol3-context-zones).

[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse]: **Automatic Prefix Reuse**: Serving systems such as SGLang index cached attention state by token prefix within a radix tree, allowing an incoming request that shares an existing token prefix to reuse cached KV blocks transparently [@zheng2024sglang]. Because radix tree lookups evaluate exact token equality rather than semantic equivalence, two requests that diverge on an early timestamp share zero cache entries past that offset. Layout discipline directly determines cache hit rates. \index{Prefix cache!radix tree}

::: {#fig-vol3-context-zones data-explore="original-context-invalidation" data-explore-key="vol3:fig-vol3-context-zones" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token**: Three consecutive requests follow the root, trunk, and leaf order of @tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ beyond the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$. A new observation changes only the leaf, so the root and trunk remain a reusable prefix. Refreshing the trunk to r18 moves the first changed token to the end of the root, and every later token is processed again. The figure assumes compatible cached state on the serving side; an identical prefix alone does not guarantee reuse." fig-alt="Three horizontal request bars labeled call n cold start, call n plus 1 new observation, and call n plus 2 trunk refreshed. Each bar has root, trunk, and leaf segments with tick marks for token positions, followed by a hatched output reserve past a dotted line labeled S max minus K max. In call n every segment is marked processed. In call n plus 1 the root and the trunk at r17 are marked prefix reused, and a red dashed line labeled first changed token sits at the leaf boundary, with the first leaf token outlined in red. In call n plus 2 only the root is reused, the trunk is at r18, and the red dashed line and outlined token sit at the root boundary. Headers name the zones above an arrow running from changes rarely to changes every call."}
![](images/svg/context_staging_layout.svg)
:::

Cache equality depends on the final serialized token sequence rather than on high-level application state. Small serialization changes (JSON key order, whitespace padding, prompt template edits, or token merges across boundaries) can quietly alter the token stream. For example, byte-pair encodings (BPE) often merge trailing whitespace with the leading characters of the next string, producing different token IDs at zone joins. Prefix stability must therefore be checked on the assembled, tokenized wire request.

An identical token prefix is necessary for cache reuse, but it is not sufficient on its own. The serving engine must also still hold compatible cache blocks in accelerator memory under the same model weights, positional encoding offsets, and attention configuration. Memory pressure, LRU eviction, or cluster autoscaling can drop cached blocks between turns even when the request prefix is byte-for-byte identical. While the serving engine manages and evicts those internal tensors, the agent runtime is responsible for keeping static material in a repeatable prefix and refreshing whatever state the next decision requires.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Prefix compatibility and the retention and eviction of cached KV blocks in the serving engine are developed in @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree.
:::

Placing fast-changing metadata near the start of a request forfeits prefix reuse for no benefit, whereas moving per-call fields (request IDs, wall-clock timestamps, step counters) into the leaf preserves reuse across the root and trunk. Whenever an early field changes, cache sharing stops at the first differing token. Consider the extreme case where the first token changes on every call, which bounds the extra cost of putting volatile fields at the front of a request.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-context-layout-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE OF A CONTEXT LAYOUT ACROSS ONE TRAJECTORY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout; fallacies; summary.
# │ Goal: Compare input bills under explicitly assumed prefix matches.
# │ Show: Uncached/reused tokens, input bills, and their ratios.
# │ How: Registry step budget; zone sizes are the selecting-policy request of
# │      calc-vol3-usable-context-budget (root = instructions + declarations,
# │      trunk = task state, leaf = selected observations).
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices; retained compatible cache; no latency estimate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class ContextLayoutPrice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    scenario = Scenarios.RepairPrefixLayoutBill  # registry step budget; scenario zone sizes
    turns = scenario.turns  # one call per turn
    root_tokens = scenario.root_tokens  # instructions + tool declarations
    trunk_tokens = scenario.trunk_tokens  # task state (constraints, record, excerpts)
    leaf_tokens = scenario.leaf_tokens  # selected observations, replaced each call
    trunk_changes = scenario.trunk_rewrites  # after the cold first call
    input_price = scenario.input_price.to(USD / Mtoken)  # hypothetical, not a provider schedule
    cached_fraction = scenario.cached_fraction

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    r = scenario.result
    context_tokens = r.request_tokens
    suffix_tokens = r.rewrite_tokens
    total_input = r.total_input
    warm_turns = r.warm_calls
    unstable_prefill = total_input
    stable_prefill = r.uncached_tokens
    stable_cached = r.cached_tokens
    hit_rate = r.hit_rate
    unstable_cost = r.unstable_cost
    stable_cost = r.stable_cost
    cost_ratio = r.cost_ratio
    prefill_ratio = r.prefill_ratio
    refresh_ratio = r.rewrite_in_leaf_calls  # trunk rewrite vs. warm call

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(warm_turns == turns - 3, "One cold call, two trunk changes, the rest leaf changes")
    check(context_tokens == 47_000, "Request equals the evidence notebook's selecting policy")
    check(refresh_ratio == 4, "A trunk rewrite costs four leaf-only calls")
    check(3 < cost_ratio < 3.5, "Unstable layout bills a little over three times the stable one")
    check(stable_prefill + stable_cached == total_input, "Every input token is billed once")
    check(0 < stable_cost < unstable_cost, "The assumed discount must reduce this input bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    turns_str = fmt_int(turns)
    root_tokens_str = fmt_int(root_tokens)
    trunk_tokens_str = fmt_int(trunk_tokens)
    leaf_tokens_str = fmt_int(leaf_tokens)
    trunk_changes_str = fmt_int(trunk_changes)
    warm_turns_str = fmt_int(warm_turns)
    price_str = fmt_usd(input_price * Mtoken, precision=0)
    cached_fraction_pct_str = fmt_percent(cached_fraction, style="prose", precision=0)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    total_input_str = fmt_int(total_input)
    prefill_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{context_tokens:,} + {trunk_changes} \times {suffix_tokens:,} + {warm_turns} \times {leaf_tokens:,} = {stable_prefill:,}".replace(
            ",", "{,}"
        )
    )
    stable_cached_str = fmt_int(stable_cached)
    hit_rate_pct_str = fmt_percent(hit_rate, style="prose", precision=1)
    unstable_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(unstable_cost, precision=2)
    stable_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(stable_cost, precision=2)
    unstable_turn_usd_str = fmt_usd(r.unstable_cost_per_call, precision=3)
    stable_turn_usd_str = fmt_usd(r.stable_cost_per_call, precision=3)
    cost_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio, precision=1)
    prefill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(prefill_ratio, precision=1)
    suffix_tokens_str = fmt_int(suffix_tokens)
    refresh_int_str = fmt_int(refresh_ratio)
```

::: {#nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout .callout-notebook title="Pricing a context layout across one trajectory"}

**Problem**: The repair agent of notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget} runs its full `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.turns_str`-turn step budget under the selecting policy, making one call per turn. Each request carries a `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.root_tokens_str`-token root of instructions and tool declarations, a `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_tokens_str`-token trunk of task state, and an `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.leaf_tokens_str`-token leaf of selected observations, measured after serialization. The leaf is replaced on each call rather than appended, and the trunk is rewritten on `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_changes_str` calls after the first, one for each compaction pass that notebook \ref{nbk-04-compaction-cadence} finds this step budget triggers. Input tokens cost a hypothetical `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.price_str` per million tokens, with cached reads billed at `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.cached_fraction_pct_str` of that price. What input bill follows from each layout?

**Variables**: Both layouts send `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.context_tokens_str` tokens per request and `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.total_input_str` input tokens across the trajectory, matching the selecting policy budget from notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}. In the unstable layout, the first token changes on every call and no prefix is reused. In the stable layout, the first call is cold, the `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_changes_str` trunk rewrites first differ right after the root, and the remaining `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.warm_turns_str` calls first differ right after the trunk, with compatible cached state kept for every matching prefix. This calculation isolates input token pricing, omitting generation charges and cache storage fees.

**Math**: The unstable layout processes all input without reuse, billing `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.unstable_cost_usd_str`. In the stable layout, the initial cold call processes the whole request, each trunk rewrite prefills the trunk and leaf, and every warm call processes only the leaf, for a total uncached volume of `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.prefill_math` tokens. The remaining `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_cached_str` tokens hit the prefix cache (`{python} ContextLayoutPrice.hit_rate_pct_str` of all input tokens). Billing uncached tokens at full price and reused tokens at the discounted rate gives `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_cost_usd_str` for the trajectory.

**Result**: Average input cost drops from `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.unstable_turn_usd_str` per call in the unstable layout to `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_turn_usd_str` in the stable layout. An unstable layout bills `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.cost_mult_str` the stable layout and requires `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.prefill_mult_str` more uncached prefill tokens. These figures are billing and token-volume ratios, not end-to-end execution speedups.

**Systems insight**: With a stable prefix, the size of the volatile leaf sets the marginal input cost of each warm call, whereas rewriting the trunk prefills `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.suffix_tokens_str` tokens, the cost of `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.refresh_int_str` leaf-only calls. Engineers should keep per-call dynamic fields in the leaf and rewrite the trunk only when workspace files or active task constraints change. That discipline lowers the input share of attempt cost in $\CostPerAcceptedTask$ by the ratio above, while keeping task accuracy ($\AcceptanceProbability$) intact because the staged context still reflects current environment state. A high cache hit rate never justifies keeping stale context.

:::

::: {#chk-04-context-hierarchy .callout-checkpoint title="Checking the staged request"}

A candidate patch has just moved the workspace from `r17` to `r18`, and the runtime is staging the next request.

- [ ] **Provenance after promotion**: If a test result moves from the leaf into a refreshed progress record, what source, version, and scope must remain attached to it?
- [ ] **Volatile fields**: Why does a changing field near the start shorten prefix reuse without necessarily eliminating it, and where should a per-call request identifier go?
- [ ] **Trunk refresh estimate**: With the layout notebook's zone sizes, how many uncached input tokens does the trajectory pay if the trunk is rewritten on every fourth call after the first instead of twice? Compare the result with the unstable layout's count.
- [ ] **Stale trunk**: After the source changes from `r17` to `r18`, why is keeping the old source in the trunk an incorrect optimization even when it raises the hit rate?

:::

Staging puts the selected evidence into a clear schema and an order built for prefix reuse, yet ordering alone does not shrink long tool outputs: an oversized test log or large source file still takes its full share of the budget. When the needed working set outgrows the available budget, the runtime must shorten the representation itself while keeping the evidence later decisions need.

## Context Compaction {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction}

As the connection-pool repair runs across turns, it accumulates repeated source listings, boilerplate test-setup output, and long execution traces. Keeping every line in every prompt uses space that later turns need for patch inspection and regression checks. Yet collapsing that trace into a bare note like "the test failed" drops the clues that matter: which revision failed, which thread schedule ran, and which assertion tripped. Compaction must shorten the working context without erasing the causal links future decisions rely on.

::: {#dfn-context-compaction .callout-definition title="Context compaction"}

***Context compaction***\index{Context compaction!definition}\index{Working-set decision!compaction} replaces material in a working context with a shorter representation chosen for the task's next decisions.

1. **Significance**: It creates room for new observations inside the fixed input allowance $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$, allowing an agent trajectory to run past the turn at which appending would overflow while retaining critical evidence, constraints, and unresolved obligations.
2. **Distinction**: A compressed representation is inherently lossy or access-deferred. Keeping a handle to omitted material makes recovery conditional on an explicit retrieval step.
3. **Common pitfall**: Assuming that a deterministic extractor, or a summary mentioning all required field names, guarantees that no decision-critical information was lost.

:::

### Choosing a compaction method {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction-method}

A regular-expression filter trims log lines deterministically, but it can drop the one line that explains an intermittent fault. A source-code outline keeps API signatures while stripping the locking logic needed to spot a missed wakeup, and an LLM-written summary can preserve high-level diagnostic intent while inventing details or misstating whether a check passed.[^fn-summary-faithfulness-audit] Different compaction methods thus trade token savings against validation work and the risk of silent information loss in different ways, and no single method fits all runtime data.

The right representation depends on the next step: checking an interface takes only an outline, whereas debugging a race condition requires full function bodies and thread-interleaving logs. Each option in @tbl-vol3-compaction-spectrum is therefore defined by what it keeps in the request and what the runtime must check, rather than by a fixed reduction ratio.

[^fn-summary-faithfulness-audit]: **Unfaithful Summaries**: In a human evaluation of neural abstractive summarizers, @maynez2020faithfulness found hallucinated content (statements unsupported by the source document) in the output of every model studied. A progress record written by a model inherits this failure mode.
